facts.raw_span: progressive unilateral skin hardening on his right thigh and buttock for 7 years
motion of his right limb joint was slightly limited
ill-defined, stony-hard plaque involving his right thigh above the patella extending to his right buttocks with loss of skin elasticity
mild hypertrichosis and hyperpigmentation
Normal results for routine blood tests
Normal results for autoantibodies, immunoglobulins, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Demonstrated slight thickening of subcutaneous tissue and T2 signal abnormality
Normal epidermis and mild pigmentation along the basal layer with subtle increase in density of fibroblasts extending to the subcutis and forming adipocyte entrapment but no evidence of inflammation
Dense reticular dermis extended below well-preserved appendages
Increased expression of CD34 in the reticular dermis
Negative Alcian blue staining

concepts.why: The patient's progressive unilateral skin hardening, ill-defined stony-hard plaque, and loss of skin elasticity are consistent with scleroderma, which is further supported by the histopathological findings of dense reticular dermis and increased expression of CD34 in the reticular dermis.

The patient's unilateral skin hardening, ill-defined plaque, and hyperpigmentation are consistent with morphea, which is further supported by the histopathological findings of dense reticular dermis and increased expression of CD34 in the reticular dermis.

The patient's progressive skin hardening, ill-defined plaque, and loss of skin elasticity are consistent with lipodermatosclerosis, which is further supported by the histopathological findings of dense reticular dermis and adipocyte entrapment.
The patient's skin hardening, ill-defined plaque, and hyperpigmentation are consistent with scleredema, which is further supported by the histopathological findings of dense reticular dermis.
It explains the increased expression of CD34 in the reticular dermis and the clinical presentation of progressive unilateral skin hardening.

rationales.F01: Unilateral skin hardening is more typical of morphea than scleroderma.
rationales.F03: The presence of a stony-hard plaque is more characteristic of morphea.
rationales.F06: The absence of abnormal autoantibodies and inflammatory markers makes scleroderma less likely.
rationales.F08: The histopathological findings of normal epidermis and increased density of fibroblasts are more consistent with morphea.
rationales.F09: The presence of dense reticular dermis extended below well-preserved appendages is more characteristic of morphea.
rationales.F10: The increased expression of CD34 in the reticular dermis is more consistent with morphea.

frontier_selector.rationale: Morphea best explains the progressive unilateral skin hardening, ill-defined plaque, mild hypertrichosis, and hyperpigmentation, with histopathological findings of normal epidermis, mild pigmentation, and increased density of fibroblasts, all without evidence of inflammation.
